title: The Canal That Broke a Nation: The French Panama Company, 1879–1893
subtitle: The French Panama Company, 1879–1893
description: Ferdinand de Lesseps conquered the Suez, but the Panamanian jungle consumed his ambition. This narrative history reconstructs the catastrophic failure of the Compagnie Universelle du Canal Interocéanique through hospital registers, company ledgers, and parliamentary inquiries. From the fatal 1879 Paris congress that ignored engineering warnings to the lottery bonds that financed a mirage, the account traces how yellow fever and financial corruption dismantled a national dream. Thousands of workers perished in the Culebra Cut while executives in Paris traded maps for balance sheets. The 1893 trial exposed a scandal reaching the Chamber of Deputies, yet these French excavations ultimately enabled the American canal. Drawing on conflicting French and Panamanian archives, this book reveals how a republic absorbed a colossal failure and transformed its ruins into a geopolitical argument. It is a definitive chronicle of hubris, disease, and the tangible remnants of an enterprise that broke a nation before building a waterway.

editorReview.text: This archival reconstruction of the French Panama Company's collapse is at its best when its disciplined structure—cross-cutting between Paris, the isthmus, and the public—is anchored by concrete evidence, from mortality registers to excavation counts. The work earns its authority through such specificity. However, the final chapters abandon this vivid, time-stamped approach for a more conventional retrospective summary, which feels like a departure from the form's core strength. Some prose patterns in the middle section also require attention, but the foundational research here is formidable.
editorReview.title: History & Social Science Editor
